title: Evolve a circuit
summary: Let blind evolution design a circuit from random wiring, then compare it with a person's design: smaller sometimes, stranger always.

links.why: design is a search through possible circuits, and evolution is one way to search
an evolved circuit opens in the studio, to be verified, laid out and exported

ideas.how: a circuit nobody understands can only be trusted after it is verified

measures.how: evolution counts gates; the transistor count shows that gates differ in size

born: Researchers start evolving circuits on computers, using the ideas of natural selection.
then: Evolutionary algorithms begin to design small digital circuits in simulation.
Adrian Thompson evolves a tone-telling circuit on a real programmable chip; it relies on physics no engineer intended.
Cartesian Genetic Programming gives a simple, standard way to evolve circuits.
Machine learning places the blocks of a real chip, and the result is published in Nature.
AI agents write and check chip code; verifying what a machine designed is the central question.

learn.plain: Imagine trying keys at random, keeping any key that opens the lock a little more than the last one, and filing it a tiny bit at random each time. After thousands of tries you have a key that works, but nobody designed it. Evolution designs circuits the same way: random wiring, keep the best copy, change it a little, repeat. It can find circuits as small as a person's, or smaller, that nobody can easily explain.
learn.engineer: Cartesian Genetic Programming encodes a feed-forward netlist as a row of nodes (function, two connections to inputs or earlier nodes) plus output pointers; inactive nodes allow neutral drift. A (1+4) evolution strategy with point mutation and acceptance of equal fitness is the standard setup. Fitness here is lexicographic: correct output bits over the full truth table (bit-parallel, one machine word per signal), then active gate count. Results are measured with the studio's synthesis, so they compare fairly with hand-written designs; gate count is not transistor count, and real evolved hardware can exploit unmodelled physics, as Thompson showed in 1996. The model leaves out timing, power and testability in the fitness.

quiz.q: How does evolution find a working circuit without understanding it?
options: It keeps random changes that are no worse, thousands of times
quiz.why: Random variation plus keeping what scores at least as well is enough to climb toward a working design.

quiz.q: Why must an evolved circuit be verified before anyone trusts it?
options: Nobody designed it, so no one can vouch for how it works
quiz.why: Without a designer's understanding, only checking every case (or a proof) shows that it is correct.
